usage: the standard 요-form to an adult you respect
반말, only to a close friend, junior, or child
hang in there a bit more
같이 includes yourself; very warm and bonding
examples: 힘내! 너는 할 수 있어.
Cheer up! You can do it.
반말 to a close friend; pairs naturally with 할 수 있어 as a classic encouragement combo
A: 너무 힘들어서 포기하고 싶어. / B: 조금만 더 힘내. 거의 다 왔잖아.
A: I want to give up, it's too hard. / B: Hang in there a little more. You're almost there.
A/B exchange showing 힘내 as a response to expressed exhaustion — this is the most common context
수술 잘 끝났대요. 아버님, 힘내세요.
They say the surgery went well. Stay strong, sir.
comforting a worried family member after medical news; 아버님 is the respectful address
nuance: 힘내세요 is built from 힘 (strength) + 내다 (to put out / summon), so literally 'summon your strength' — you are urging someone to gather energy and push through something hard, not merely sympathizing. It is an active forward push, not passive comfort. Compare it with 괜찮아요 (it's okay), which only soothes; 힘내세요 is the right call before or during a struggle (exam, illness, job loss), whereas pure condolence like 안타깝네요 fits once everything is over. It collocates naturally with 조금만 더 ('just a little more') and 같이 ('together'). Register is crucial: dropping to bare 힘내 with a senior sounds like an order from below — keep the -세요 upward. For very mild setbacks, the breezy 파이팅! lands better; 힘내세요 implies the person is in real hardship and can feel overwrought for a small disappointment.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'summon your strength' (힘 = strength, 내다 = put out). The real meaning is an active forward push to keep going through hardship — not just 'I feel for you,' but 'you can get through this.' It belongs in the middle of a struggle, not after it has ended.

Use it with someone facing a real ordeal: an exam, illness, job hunt, or emotional low point. Polite 힘내세요 to anyone you respect; drop to 힘내 only with close friends, juniors, or children — bare 힘내 to a boss or teacher sounds presumptuous, like an order from below.

괜찮아요 ('it's okay') comforts but does not push forward. 파이팅!/화이팅! is a lighter energetic cheer for mild situations or sports-style pump-up. 안타깝네요 ('what a shame') is pure sympathy, right for loss with no path forward. 힘내세요 uniquely combines empathy with an active forward urge.
힘내 (반말) → 힘내요 (neutral polite) → 힘내세요 (polite, standard) → 조금만 더 힘내세요 (softened, 'almost there') → 우리 같이 힘내요 (inclusive, 'let's both keep going').

'Cheer up' in English is light and casual — it can be said for mild frustration. 힘내세요 implies a genuine, significant struggle; using it for a trivial complaint feels overdramatic. Also, never drop to 힘내 with anyone older or in a position above you — it will read as disrespectful.

mistakes: Saying 힘내 to a senior or boss
힘내 is 반말 and sounds like an order aimed downward. To anyone you respect, always keep the polite -세요: 힘내세요.
Using 힘내세요 for mild, passing disappointment
It implies a genuine ordeal worth mustering strength for; for a small letdown it overdramatizes. A casual 파이팅! or 괜찮아요 fits better.
Translating 'cheer up' as 기뻐하세요
기뻐하세요 commands someone to literally feel joy, which is unnatural and pushy. The set phrase for encouragement is 힘내세요.

usage: 반말 to a friend, junior, or child
참 has a warm, slightly childlike ring — classic for children
examples: 우와, 잘했어! 진짜 대단하다.
Wow, well done! That's seriously impressive.
반말 reacting to a friend's small win; 대단하다 is a natural follow-up
A: 발표 어땠어요? 떨렸는데. / B: 잘했어요. 준비 많이 한 게 느껴졌어요.
A: How was my presentation? I was so nervous. / B: You did great. I could tell you prepared a lot.
A/B exchange — the most natural context, praising effort that shows in a result
혼자 이걸 다 해냈어요? 정말 잘했어요.
You finished all this alone? You really did well.
praising someone's independence with genuine surprise; 해냈다 (managed to do) strengthens the sense of achievement
nuance: 잘했어요 is 잘 (well) + 했어요 (past of 하다), so the past tense is the whole point: you are judging a result that is already finished. It cannot logically come before an event — for encouragement before the fact use 잘할 거예요 or 화이팅. Compare it with 잘하네요 (present, admiring an ongoing skill as you watch: 'you're good at this') and 잘하셨어요 (past with honorific -시-, for elders). The key social caution: Korean praise flows comfortably downward — to juniors, peers, and children — but praising a boss or elder with 잘했어요 sounds like you are grading them from a superior position. Toward a senior, Koreans shift to 수고하셨어요 or 잘 보고 들었습니다 to avoid the evaluator role. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'good job' as socially flat, the way it often is in English — in Korean, knowing which direction to aim the praise is as important as the words themselves.

structuredNuance.t: 잘 (well) + 했어요 (past of 하다). The past tense is not incidental — it signals you are evaluating a completed result, not wishing future success. Use it only after the task is fully done.

Natural for praising a peer, junior, student, or child on a finished task — a presentation, an exam result, a DIY project. To a boss or elder, 잘했어요 sounds like you outrank them; swap to 수고하셨어요 or 잘 보고 들었습니다 for upward praise.

잘하네요 (present tense) admires an ongoing skill as you watch it. 잘할 거예요 encourages before the fact. 수고하셨어요 thanks effort without evaluating quality — right for peers and seniors. 잘했어요 is the only one that evaluates a completed result as 'good.'
잘했어 (반말) → 잘했어요 (polite) → 잘하셨어요 (with honorific -시-, for respected elders) → 정말 잘했어요 → 참 잘했어요 (extra warmth, often for children).

English 'good job' flows freely upward (you can tell your boss 'good job' casually). In Korean, 잘했어요 carries an evaluator-to-subject direction that makes it uncomfortable aimed at a senior. Also: never say it before the task starts — that is a logic error in Korean.

mistakes: Saying 잘했어요 before a task is finished
The past tense judges a completed result; said beforehand it's illogical. Encourage with 잘할 거예요 or 화이팅 instead.
Praising your boss with 잘했어요
Evaluating a superior's work sounds like you outrank them. Toward a senior, use 수고하셨습니다 or express thanks rather than a grade.
Confusing 잘했어요 with 잘하셨어요 for elders
To a respected adult, drop in the honorific -시-: 잘하셨어요. Plain 잘했어요 to an elder can feel a touch flat or familiar.

english: Good work. / Thanks for your effort.
usage: to a peer or junior after shared effort
thank you for your hard work
많다 adds 'a lot of' effort; extra warmth
to someone still working as you leave — context-dependent
examples: 수고했어, 오늘 고마웠어.
Good work, thanks for today.
반말 to a close colleague after a long shift; the most natural end-of-day sign-off with a friend
A: 다들 오늘 정말 열심히 했어요. / B: 네, 다들 수고하셨어요. 들어가서 쉬세요.
A: Everyone really worked hard today. / B: Yes, everyone did. Go home and rest.
A/B team wrap-up exchange; the team lead uses 수고하셨어요 with -시- to honor the group
이사 도와줘서 정말 수고하셨어요.
Thank you so much for helping me move.
thanking someone after genuinely tiring, selfless help; the effort focus of 수고하셨어요 makes this feel more sincere than just 감사해요
nuance: 수고 is Sino-Korean 受苦 (receive-suffering), so 수고했어요 literally acknowledges that someone has taken on toil and trouble on your behalf — it honors the effort itself, not whether the outcome was good. A project can fail and still earn a heartfelt 수고했어요 for the work poured in, which is what separates it from 잘했어요 (good result). It collocates naturally with 많이, 오늘도, and 정말. The register trap: a beginner often reads 'never say 수고 to a boss,' but the actual rule is more precise — bare 수고했어요 (peer-to-peer level) aimed upward is too familiar; the fully honorific 수고하셨습니다 or 수고하셨어요 is widely used to seniors in modern Korean workplaces and sounds respectful. What truly grates upward is 수고하세요 ('keep on working'), which can read as 'you keep slaving away' — never say this to a superior. The English-speaker pitfall is using the casual form everywhere after hearing it so often; always gauge the rank relationship first.

structuredNuance.t: 수고 (受苦) = 'receiving hardship'; the full expression thanks someone for the toil they took on, not the quality of the result. A failed project still earns a genuine 수고했어요 — this empathy-over-outcome sense is what makes it warm and distinct.

After a shared task ends — end of shift, end of a project, after someone helped you move or cook. Peer/junior: 수고했어요. Senior: 수고하셨어요 or 수고하셨습니다 (add -시-). Never use bare 수고했어요 to a boss; never say 수고하세요 to a superior as you leave.

잘했어요 judges the result (good outcome). 고생하셨어요 also means 'you went through hardship' and is slightly more sympathetic — often used after genuinely grueling work (moving, a long trip, overtime). 수고했어요 is the everyday catch-all for effort; 고생하셨어요 carries a slightly heavier weight of real struggle.
수고했어 (반말) → 수고했어요 (peer/junior) → 수고하셨어요 (honorific, safe) → 수고하셨습니다 (most formal) → 수고 많았어요 ('you worked really hard').

English 'thanks for your hard work' is socially flat. In Korean, the register split is sharp: using casual 수고했어요 to a senior is too familiar, and 수고하세요 to a departing boss can sound like 'you keep toiling.' When in doubt about rank, default to 수고하셨습니다.

mistakes: Saying bare 수고했어요 to a clear senior
Without -시- it carries a peer-to-junior tone that feels too familiar upward. Use 수고하셨습니다 or 수고하셨어요 for seniors.
Telling your boss 수고하세요 as you leave first
To a superior it can sound like 'you keep working away,' faintly cheeky. Better: 먼저 들어가 보겠습니다 / 먼저 가 보겠습니다.
Using 수고했어요 to praise the quality of a result
It thanks effort, not achievement; for a good result say 잘했어요 (downward) or 고생하셨습니다. Mixing the two blurs your meaning.

usage: general warning about a hazard, polite
to someone heading out — a caring farewell
noun + 조심: the hazard comes first, then 조심하세요
fixed compound — careful with your words
examples: 뜨거우니까 조심해.
It's hot, so be careful.
반말 handing hot food to a close friend; -니까 gives the causal reason
A: 퇴근해요. 먼저 갈게요. / B: 네, 길이 미끄러우니 조심히 가세요.
A: I'm heading out. I'll go first. / B: Okay, the roads are slippery, so get home safely.
A/B farewell exchange — the most typical context for 조심히 가세요 in daily life
밤늦었는데 조심히 들어가세요.
It's late at night, so get home safely.
seeing a guest off at the door; 들어가세요 ('go inside') is the natural verb when heading home
nuance: 조심 is Sino-Korean 操心 ('handle the heart / keep one's mind alert'), so 조심하세요 tells someone to stay watchful and avoid harm. It operates in two very different modes: as a real-time warning before a specific danger (slippery floor, boiling pot), or as a warm farewell closer to English 'take care.' For the warning mode, Korean fronts the danger noun — 발 조심하세요 (watch your step), 감기 조심하세요 (mind the cold), 차 조심하세요 (watch the traffic) — and leaving the noun out sounds vague. For the farewell mode, 조심히 가세요 or 조심히 들어가세요 is the set phrase, where 조심히 (adverb) modifies the verb of going. Note these two forms are not interchangeable: 조심히 가세요 does not warn; 조심하세요 without a destination verb does not work as a goodbye. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'be careful' as a reflexive parting phrase the way English does — a bare 조심하세요 without context or the farewell verb pattern sounds abrupt or alarming rather than warm.

structuredNuance.t: 조심 (操心) = 'manage your heart/mind'; the real meaning is 'stay alert and avoid harm.' Two distinct uses: (1) a real-time warning before a specific hazard, and (2) a warm farewell wish for someone's safe journey — these are not interchangeable in form.

Warning: say it when someone is about to encounter a specific danger (hot food, icy steps, heavy traffic). Farewell: say 조심히 가세요 / 조심히 들어가세요 as a caring send-off. Both forms work politely to adults; drop to 조심해 only with close friends or juniors.

안전하게 가세요 ('go safely') is a slightly more formal farewell, common in written messages. 조심해요 is the neutral polite form of the warning. 조심히 가세요 is the warm spoken farewell specifically for the person departing. 잘 가세요 ('go well') is lighter and broader, not focused on safety.
조심해 (반말 warning) → 조심하세요 (polite warning) → 조심히 가세요 (farewell, going out) → 조심히 들어가세요 (farewell, going home) → [위험 명사] 조심하세요 (named hazard).

Two traps: first, forgetting to front the danger noun (Koreans say 감기 조심하세요, not just 조심하세요 for 'watch out for colds'). Second, using bare 조심하세요 as a casual goodbye — without either a named hazard or the farewell verb pattern (가세요 / 들어가세요), it sounds abrupt or alarming rather than warm.

mistakes: Dropping the object when there is a specific hazard
Bare 조심하세요 leaves the danger unnamed and sounds vague. Front it: 발 조심하세요, 감기 조심하세요, 차 조심하세요.
Saying 감기를 조심하세요 with 를
Colloquially the noun attaches directly without a particle — 감기 조심하세요. Over-marking with 을/를 sounds stiff and textbook-like.
Using 조심히 as if it were a standalone command
조심히 is an adverb needing a movement verb: 조심히 가세요, 조심히 들어가세요. The standalone command form is 조심하세요, not 조심히.

usage: warm and polite, said before a challenge
-ㅂ니다 for written notes or formal contexts
-ㄹ게요 promises ongoing support on your behalf
반말 to a close friend before an event
examples: 내일 시험이지? 행운을 빌어!
Your exam's tomorrow, right? Good luck!
반말 cheering on a friend the night before
A: 내일 면접인데 너무 떨려요. / B: 잘 하실 수 있어요. 행운을 빌어요!
A: I have an interview tomorrow and I'm so nervous. / B: You'll do great. I'm wishing you luck!
A/B exchange — the natural context: one person shares anxiety, the other responds with encouragement + this phrase
새 가게 잘되길 바라요. 진심으로 행운을 빕니다.
I hope your new shop thrives. I sincerely wish you good luck.
formal, heartfelt send-off; 진심으로 elevates the sincerity for a big life milestone
nuance: 행운 is Sino-Korean 幸運 ('fortunate-luck'), and 빌다 here means to pray or wish, so 행운을 빌어요 is literally 'I pray for your good fortune' — a sincere, warm hope that chance will favor someone before an exam, interview, audition, or big decision. The object particle 을 (행운을) is part of the set phrase and should not be dropped. Contrast it with 화이팅!/파이팅!, which is a breezy, energetic cheer focused on spirit and effort — Koreans actually shout 화이팅 far more often in everyday life; 행운을 빌어요 is gentler, more formal, and specifically about luck and outcome rather than hustle. Note that 빌다 also means 'to borrow' in the form 빌리다 — these are distinct verbs, so the sentence cannot be misread as 'I'll borrow your luck.' The timing is everything: 행운을 빌어요 belongs strictly before the event; after results are known, switch to 축하해요 (congratulations) or 아쉽네요 / 다음엔 잘 될 거예요 (too bad, better luck next time).

structuredNuance.t: 행운 (幸運) = 'fortunate luck'; 빌다 = 'to pray/wish.' Literally 'I pray for your good fortune.' The real use is a sincere, heartfelt pre-event wish — warmer and more formal than a casual cheer, genuinely pointing at luck and chance rather than just effort.

Use it the day before or moment before an exam, interview, audition, competition, or major decision. Polite 빌어요 for most situations; bump to 빕니다 in written messages or formal settings. Drop to 빌어 only with close friends. Always pre-event — it makes no sense once results are out.

화이팅!/파이팅! is a far more common spoken cheer, focused on effort, energy, and fighting spirit — it is casual and punchy. 행운을 빌어요 is quieter, points at luck/outcome, and sounds slightly more formal and sincere. 잘될 거예요 ('it'll go well') is reassurance based on optimism, not a luck-wish.
행운을 빌어 (반말) → 행운을 빌어요 (polite) → 행운을 빌게요 ('I'll keep wishing you luck') → 행운을 빕니다 (formal/written) → 진심으로 행운을 빕니다 (sincerest, for big milestones).

English 'good luck' can be casual, throwaway, or even sarcastic. 행운을 빌어요 is always genuinely sincere and can only precede the event — using it after results land sounds strange. Also, Koreans in daily speech much more often shout 화이팅! rather than 행운을 빌어요; over-relying on this phrase sounds bookish when a casual situation calls for 화이팅.

mistakes: Saying 행운을 빌어요 after the event is over
It hopes for a future outcome, so it only fits beforehand. After the fact use 축하해요 (good news) or 수고했어요 / 아쉽네요.
Dropping the particle: 행운 빌어요
The set phrase keeps the object marker — 행운을 빌어요. Omitting 을 sounds clipped and grammatically incomplete.
Confusing prayer-빌다 with borrow-빌리다
행운을 빌어요 uses 빌다 (to pray/wish for). 빌리다 means to borrow and is a completely different verb; don't blend them.

usage: raises the listener — for elders, bosses, formal joy
warm and equal, to a peer or friend
진심으로 = sincerely, for big milestones like weddings or promotions
생신 is the honorific word for birthday
examples: 합격 축하해! 한턱 쏴.
Congrats on passing! Treat us.
반말 ribbing a friend about standing a round
A: 오늘 아들이 대학에 합격했대요. / B: 어머, 정말요? 진심으로 축하드려요!
A: I heard your son got into university today. / B: Oh my, really? Heartfelt congratulations!
A/B exchange — sharing good family news; 드려요 is natural here because the parent being congratulated is an elder
승진 축하드립니다, 부장님. 정말 잘되셨어요.
Congratulations on your promotion, sir. I'm so glad for you.
to a superior, fully formal -ㅂ니다 + 부장님; 잘되셨어요 uses honorific -시-
nuance: 축하 is Sino-Korean 祝賀 ('celebrate-congratulate'), and the critical split is in the verb: 축하해요 uses plain 하다 (to do), while 축하드려요 replaces it with 드리다 ('to humbly give/offer'), elevating the listener. So 축하드려요 is 'I humbly offer you my congratulations' — the humble verb lifts the other person socially. Use it without hesitation for bosses, parents, in-laws, teachers, and wedding guests who are your seniors. The event is fronted as a bare noun: 결혼 축하, 합격 축하, 승진 축하 — not 합격을 축하해요, which sounds overly grammatical. Remember to swap 생일 for the honorific 생신 when the birthday person is a senior. Contrast 축하드려요 with 잘됐어요 ('that worked out great'), which is informal celebration for a good outcome but not a formal congratulation. The English-speaker pitfall is using flat casual 축하해 with a senior or at a formal event — that sounds startlingly blunt; always ask yourself whether 드려요 or 합니다 is appropriate before speaking.

structuredNuance.t: 축하 (祝賀) = 'celebrate-congratulate'; 드리다 = 'to give humbly.' The real effect: by choosing 드리다 over 하다, you lower yourself and raise the listener — the same humble mechanism as 드세요 ('please eat') vs 먹어요. It transforms a peer-level phrase into a respectful one.

To a peer or friend: 축하해요 / 축하해. To a senior, boss, elder, or in a formal setting (wedding toast, promotion announcement): 축하드려요 or 축하드립니다. For a senior's birthday specifically: 생신 축하드려요 (생신, not 생일). Never use bare 축하해 upward.

축하해요 (plain, peer-level) vs 축하드려요 (humble, senior-level) — same warmth, different social altitude. 잘됐어요 ('great that it worked out') is casual celebration of a good outcome but not a formal congratulation. 수고하셨어요 thanks effort; 축하드려요 celebrates a positive result.
축하해 (반말) → 축하해요 (polite peer) → 축하드려요 (humble-polite, senior) → 축하드립니다 (most formal) → 진심으로 축하드립니다 (sincerest). Event noun fronted: 합격 / 결혼 / 승진 + 축하드려요.

English 'congratulations' is socially flat — you can say it to anyone at any register. In Korean, defaulting to casual 축하해 with a boss or elder is jarringly familiar. Also, Korean fronts the event (합격 축하해요), unlike English 'congrats on passing' — resist adding an extra particle between the event noun and 축하.

mistakes: Using casual 축하해 toward a senior or boss
반말-level 축하해 sounds disrespectful on a happy occasion. Use the humble 축하드려요 or 축하드립니다.
Saying 생일 축하드려요 to an elder
For a senior, 생일 becomes the honorific 생신: 생신 축하드려요. Using plain 생일 to an elder is a missed courtesy.
Inserting a particle: 합격을 축하해요
Colloquial Korean fronts the event directly without a particle — 합격 축하해요. Adding 을/를 here sounds stiff and textbook-like.

english: It is cool. / You look great.
usage: you're so impressive / you look wonderful
honorific -시- about or to a respected person
examples: 우와, 그 재킷 진짜 멋있어!
Whoa, that jacket's seriously cool!
반말 complimenting a friend's outfit; 진짜 is the everyday intensifier
A: 저 오늘 발표 어땠어요? / B: 발표하시는 모습이 정말 멋있었어요.
A: How was my presentation today? / B: You looked really impressive up there.
A/B exchange — praising someone's manner and presence, not just the content; 모습 = 'the way they looked/appeared'
혼자 세계여행을 하셨다니, 정말 멋있으세요.
You traveled the world alone? You're genuinely amazing.
admiring a person's life decision with honorific 멋있으세요 — the -시- is what makes it respectful rather than patronizing
nuance: 멋있어요 comes from 멋 (style, flair, class) + 있어요 (to have), literally 'to have flair' — it praises whatever strikes you as stylish, impressive, admirable, or awe-inspiring: a look, a skill, a bold decision, a person's whole presence. Because it is built on 있다 (not 하다), its past is 멋있었어요 and the honorific is 멋있으세요 — knowing this pattern removes all conjugation worry. Contrast with 예뻐요 (pretty/cute-beautiful, focused on visual appeal) and 잘생겼어요 (good-looking/handsome, specifically about a person's face and physique): those judge surface appearance alone, while 멋있어요 also reaches inner character and competence — a wise speech or a courageous act is 멋있다 but not 예쁘다. In casual speech 멋지다 / 멋져요 is a common synonym, slightly more energetic in tone. The big English-speaker pitfall is the near-homophone 맛있어요 ('tasty,' from 맛 = taste): 멋 (first vowel ㅓ, 'uh') vs 맛 (first vowel ㅏ, 'ah') differ by one vowel and swapping them changes 'you're so cool' into 'you're so delicious.'

structuredNuance.t: 멋 (flair/style) + 있어요 (to have) = 'to have flair.' The real scope is wide: you can call a stylish outfit, a skillful performance, a brave decision, or a person's whole aura 멋있다. It is admiration that goes beyond surface looks.

Use freely to peers and friends: 멋있어 (반말), 멋있어요 (polite). To a respected person you admire — a teacher, an older person, someone you look up to — use 멋있으세요 (honorific -시-). Calling a senior or boss 귀여워요 is condescending; 멋있으세요 to them is flattering.

예뻐요 = refined surface beauty (a flower, a dress, a woman's looks). 잘생겼어요 = physical attractiveness, mainly for men's faces. 멋있어요 = stylish coolness + impressiveness + inner character. 멋지다 / 멋져요 = casual synonym, slightly more energetic. Only 멋있어요 can praise a courageous decision or an impressive skill.
멋있어 (반말) → 멋있어요 (polite) → 멋있으세요 (honorific) → 정말 멋있어요 → 멋있었어요 (past). Synonym track: 멋지다 → 멋져요 (casual spoken).

Critical near-homophone: 맛있어요 ('tasty,' from 맛 = taste). The vowels differ — 멋 (ㅓ) vs 맛 (ㅏ) — but in fast speech they sound very close. Keep 멋 for style and impressiveness, 맛 for flavor and food. Swapping them turns a compliment into something very strange.

mistakes: Confusing 멋있어요 (cool) with 맛있어요 (tasty)
Only the vowel differs — 멋 (style) vs 맛 (taste). Say 멋있어요 to praise coolness; 맛있어요 is strictly for food.
Using 멋있어요 where you mean simply 'pretty'
멋있어요 admires style and impressiveness, not surface prettiness alone. For refined beauty use 예뻐요; for physical attractiveness use 잘생겼어요.
Conjugating it like a 하다 verb, e.g. 멋있해요
It follows the 있다 adjective pattern: present 멋있어요, past 멋있었어요. There is no 하다 in it.

usage: 너무 = 'so/too,' the most natural intensifier here
반말 to a friend or about an animal
plain exclamation blurted aloud or in a chat caption
examples: 어머, 너무 귀여워!
Oh my, so cute!
반말 reaction on seeing a puppy; 어머 is a soft, affectionate 'oh my'
A: 조카가 말을 배우기 시작했대요. / B: 아, 그 나이가 제일 귀여워요!
A: My niece started learning to talk. / B: Oh, that age is the cutest!
A/B exchange — sharing good family news; reacting with 귀여워요 about a toddler is the most typical daily use
고양이가 발로 세수해요. 진짜 귀엽다.
The cat washes its face with its paw. So cute.
plain-form 귀엽다 as a caption or a comment to oneself — very common in texting and social media
nuance: 귀여워요 reacts to something small, charming, and lovable — babies, pets, plushies, a child's small actions. It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: the stem 귀엽- drops its ㅂ before vowel endings and adds 워, giving 귀여워요 (never 귀엽어요) and past 귀여웠어요. The same flip happens with 춥다 → 추워요 (cold), 덥다 → 더워요 (hot), 무겁다 → 무거워요 (heavy) — mastering 귀엽다 unlocks a whole conjugation class. Contrast 귀엽다 with 예쁘다 (pretty, elegant beauty) and 아름답다 (beautiful, grand): 귀엽다 is specifically about adorable, often youthful or petite charm, while 예쁘다 covers refined loveliness. The key social caution: calling a senior or authority figure 귀여워요 is condescending — it infantilizes them. English 'cute' gets aimed at people of all ages casually, but in Korean that can land badly; keep 귀엽다 for children, pets, peers you're close to, and romantic partners.

structuredNuance.t: 귀엽다 is a pure native Korean adjective meaning 'adorable/endearing.' The real range: small animals, babies, toddlers, tiny or petite things, and — in romantic contexts — a partner's charming behavior. It is about small-scale, youthful, lovable cuteness, not broad beauty.

Use freely for animals, children, plushies, and charming small actions. To a peer friend about their behavior it is affectionate. To a romantic partner it is a compliment. Never to a senior or someone you respect — it reads as condescending or infantilizing. 반말 귀여워 to a close friend is fine.

예쁘다 = refined, elegant beauty (a woman's looks, a flower, a dress). 아름답다 = grand, scenic, or deeply moving beauty. 귀엽다 = adorable, small-scale, youthful cuteness. These do not overlap much — a puppy is 귀엽다, not 아름답다; a mountain view is 아름답다, not 귀엽다.
ㅂ-irregular: 귀엽다 → 귀여워요 (present) → 귀여웠어요 (past) → 귀여울 것 같아요 ('seems like it'll be cute'). Same flip as 춥다 → 추워요, 덥다 → 더워요. Intensified: 너무 귀여워요, 정말 귀여워요.

Two traps: (1) conjugating it as 귀엽어요 — wrong, the ㅂ drops and becomes 워: 귀여워요; (2) directing it at a senior the way English 'cute' freely applies across ages — in Korean 귀여워요 to a boss or elder is patronizing. Also note: the wrong form 귀엽어요 is one of the most common written errors.

mistakes: Saying 귀엽어요 instead of 귀여워요
귀엽다 is ㅂ-irregular: ㅂ becomes 우/워 before a vowel ending → 귀여워요, past 귀여웠어요. 귀엽어요 is incorrect.
Calling a senior or boss 귀여워요
To someone you should respect it sounds patronizing and infantilizing. Reserve 귀엽다 for kids, pets, peers, or a romantic partner.
Using 귀여워요 to mean elegant beauty
귀엽다 is adorable/endearing, not refined-pretty. For graceful beauty use 예뻐요; for grand or moving beauty use 아름다워요.

usage: polite, said as food is served or presented
-십시오 in restaurant or formal service settings
the warm host's urging to eat more
반말 to a close friend or family junior
examples: 자, 맛있게 먹어! 많이 먹어.
Here, enjoy! Eat lots.
반말 setting food in front of a close friend; 많이 먹어 is the natural follow-up
A: 주문하신 음식 나왔습니다. / B: 맛있게 드세요.
A: Here is your order. / B: Enjoy your meal.
A/B restaurant exchange — this is exactly when 맛있게 드세요 is used: a server or host presenting food; the diner doesn't say it
제가 직접 만들었어요. 입에 맞으면 좋겠어요. 맛있게 드세요.
I made it myself. I hope it suits your taste. Please enjoy.
a host serving home-cooked food to a guest; 입에 맞으면 좋겠어요 is a common humble accompaniment
nuance: 맛있게 드세요 breaks down as 맛있게 (adverb from 맛있다: 'deliciously') + 드세요 (honorific of 먹다: 'eat'), so it literally means 'eat it deliciously' — a kind wish that the listener enjoys the food. Crucially this is a host or server line, directed at the people who are about to eat; you never say it about your own eating. Compare 드세요 with 잡수세요: both are honorific forms of 먹다, but 잡수세요 is reserved for grandparents and the very elderly, whereas 드세요 is the standard polite default across generations. The counterpart lines for the diner are 잘 먹겠습니다 (before eating, 'I will eat well, thank you') and 잘 먹었습니다 (after, 'that was a great meal, thank you') — these are the expressions of gratitude toward the cook or host. There is no direct native English equivalent for 맛있게 드세요 (bon appétit is borrowed French in English), so English speakers often go quiet at the table — learning this phrase is a small but very natural-sounding Korean courtesy.

structuredNuance.t: 맛있게 (adverb: 'deliciously') + 드세요 (honorific eat). Literally 'eat it deliciously.' The real meaning is a host or server's warm wish that you enjoy the food — it is directed outward at the eater, never self-directed.

Said by the person presenting or serving food — a server, a host, a cook — to the people about to eat. Use 맛있게 드세요 as the standard polite form; 드십시오 in formal restaurant settings; 맛있게 먹어 only in 반말 to close friends or family juniors.

많이 드세요 ('please eat a lot') is the host's urging to eat more — warmer and more insistent, common from Korean hosts who want guests to eat heartily. 잘 먹겠습니다 is the diner's pre-meal thanks; 잘 먹었습니다 the post-meal thanks. 잡수세요 is the more deferential honorific for eating, reserved for grandparents and the elderly.
맛있게 먹어 (반말) → 맛있게 먹어요 (neutral polite) → 맛있게 드세요 (polite default) → 맛있게 드십시오 (formal service) → 많이 드세요 (host's urging). The diner's counterpart: 잘 먹겠습니다 (before) / 잘 먹었습니다 (after).

Two traps: (1) saying it about your own eating — it is aimed at the listener, not yourself; for your own meal say 잘 먹겠습니다 before and 잘 먹었습니다 after; (2) using plain 먹어 to a guest or elder — 먹다 is too casual for anyone you are serving; use the honorific 드세요 or 잡수세요 (for grandparents).

mistakes: Saying 맛있게 드세요 about your own meal
It wishes the listener enjoyment, so it's aimed at others. As the one eating, say 잘 먹겠습니다 before and 잘 먹었습니다 after.
Using plain 먹어/먹으세요 to a guest or elder
먹다 is the plain verb; to someone you serve and respect use the honorific 드세요 (or 잡수세요 for the elderly).
Expecting it to mean 'thanks for the food'
맛있게 드세요 is the server/host's offer, not the diner's thanks. To thank the cook, use 잘 먹겠습니다 / 잘 먹었습니다.

usage: rising intonation = question; polite check-in with someone you know
how are you getting on these days?
어떻게 asks 'how,' more open-ended, invites detail
falling intonation = the answer; same phrase, opposite tone
examples: 야, 잘 지내? 요즘 어때?
Hey, doing okay? How are things lately?
반말 checking in on a friend; 요즘 어때? is the natural follow-up to invite sharing
A: 오랜만이에요! 그동안 잘 지내셨어요? / B: 네, 덕분에 잘 지냈어요. 선생님은요?
A: Long time no see! Have you been well? / B: Yes, I've been fine, thanks. And you, teacher?
A/B reunion exchange — honorific 지내셨어요 toward a teacher; answering with 덕분에 ('thanks to you') is the polite Korean formula
부모님도 다 잘 지내시죠?
Your parents are doing well too, right?
asking about someone's family; honorific 지내시죠 = 지내세요 + 죠 (seeking confirmation); shows warmth and care
nuance: 잘 지내요 pairs 잘 (well) with 지내다, a verb meaning 'to get along / pass one's days / spend time living,' so it asks about a span of time — how has life been going lately? — not a single instant. It is far closer to 'how have you been keeping?' than a snapshot 'how do you feel right now?' Intonation alone turns question into answer: a rising pitch makes it 잘 지내요?, a falling pitch makes it 잘 지내요. Contrast it with 어떻게 지내요? (more open-ended, invites details, no built-in presumption) and 기분이 어때요? ('how do you feel?', probing mood in the moment, not life span). Because it implies a stretch of time, the past form 잘 지냈어요? is especially natural when reconnecting after a gap. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it like American 'How are you?' which functions as a ritual greeting to strangers in English; in Korean 잘 지내요? implies you know the person and are genuinely reconnecting — directing it at a shop clerk or a stranger you just met sounds oddly familiar.

structuredNuance.t: 잘 (well) + 지내다 (to pass one's days / get along in life). The real meaning spans a period of time — 'how has life been going?' — not a snapshot feeling. Intonation alone flips it: rising = question (잘 지내요?), falling = answer (잘 지내요.).

Use it when reconnecting with someone you already know — a friend you haven't seen in a while, a former colleague, a classmate. For a senior: 잘 지내세요? (with honorific -시-). After a long absence: past form 잘 지냈어요? To a stranger you have just met: don't use it; just say 안녕하세요.

어떻게 지내요? ('how are you getting on?') is more open-ended and invites a longer answer — no built-in presumption of 'fine.' 기분이 어때요? asks about mood right now, not life in general. 잘 있어요? ('are you okay?') checks whether someone is in a safe situation, not how life is going.
잘 지내? (반말) → 잘 지내요? (polite) → 잘 지내세요? (honorific, for seniors) → 잘 지냈어요? (past, after a gap) → 잘 지내셨어요? (past + honorific). Polite answer: 네, 덕분에 잘 지내요.

American 'How are you?' is a social ritual said to strangers and cashiers with no real expectation of an answer. 잘 지내요? implies prior acquaintance and genuine reconnection — using it with a stranger or a shop clerk sounds oddly intimate. With anyone unfamiliar, 안녕하세요 alone is the correct greeting.

mistakes: Using 잘 지내요? as a greeting to a stranger
It presumes prior acquaintance and reconnection. For someone you just met, 안녕하세요 is the right greeting; save 잘 지내요? for people you already know.
Saying 잘 있어요? when you mean 'how have you been?'
있다 asks location/existence ('are you there/around?'), not how life is going. The set phrase for well-being over time is 잘 지내요?
Dropping the honorific for a senior: plain 잘 지내요? to an elder
To someone you respect, add -시-: 잘 지내세요? / 잘 지내셨어요? Plain 잘 지내요? can feel a touch too casual upward.

usage: 정말 adds genuine surprise or feeling
examples: 어? 오랜만이야! 잘 지냈어?
Oh? Long time no see! Have you been well?
반말 running into a friend unexpectedly; 잘 지냈어? is the natural follow-up question
A: 우리 거의 일 년 만이에요. / B: 맞아요, 정말 오랜만이에요. 그동안 잘 지내셨어요?
A: It's been almost a year for us. / B: That's right, it really has been a while. Have you been well?
A/B reunion exchange — the most typical scenario, with 만 marking the elapsed time and 잘 지내셨어요 as the polite follow-up
오랜만에 뵙겠습니다, 선배님.
It's been a long time, senior. (formal)
humble 뵙겠습니다 (humble form of 보다) + 선배님; this is the respectful way to greet a senior after an absence
nuance: 오랜만이에요 is 오랜만 ('a long while since,' from 오래 = long time + 만 = elapsed-interval marker) + 이에요 (to be), so it states 'it is the case that a long time has passed' — a complete sentence said the moment you reunite. The interval marker 만 is the key structural piece: 일 년 만에 (after a full year), 몇 달 만에 (after several months), 오랜만에 (after a long time) — it measures elapsed duration. Do not confuse 오랜만이에요 (the greeting sentence, with 이에요) and the adverb 오랜만에 ('after a long time,' which needs a following verb — 오랜만에 만나요, 오랜만에 영화 봤어요). Using the adverb form 오랜만에 as a bare greeting is a classic learner mistake. For a senior, raise the verb: 오랜만에 뵙겠습니다 uses the humble form 뵙다 instead of 보다. The English-speaker pitfall is applying 'long time no see' loosely for any gap — in Korean 오랜만이에요 genuinely implies weeks or months have passed; used for someone you saw a few days ago it sounds sarcastic.

structuredNuance.t: 오랜만 (오래 + 만 = 'a long elapsed interval') + 이에요 = 'it is a long time since (we met).' The real use: a warm greeting at the moment of reunion after a genuinely long absence — weeks or months, not days. It is a declarative sentence, not just an exclamation.

Said at the moment of reunion after a long absence. Polite 이에요 for peers and adults. For seniors: use 오랜만입니다 and follow up with 오랜만에 뵙겠습니다 (humble 뵙다). 반말: 오랜만이야. Reserve the phrase for genuine gaps — weeks or months, not a few days.

오랜만이에요 is the complete greeting sentence. 오랜만에 is the adverb ('after a long time') that must be followed by a verb: 오랜만에 만나요, 오랜만에 봤어요. These two are not interchangeable. 久しぶり in Japanese is the functional equivalent, if that helps as a parallel.
오랜만이야 (반말) → 오랜만이에요 (polite) → 정말 오랜만이에요 → 오랜만입니다 (formal) → 오랜만에 뵙겠습니다 (humble, for senior). Adverb track: 오랜만에 + verb.

English 'long time no see' can be used casually for gaps of a few days, even sarcastically. In Korean 오랜만이에요 implies a real stretch of weeks or months; using it after seeing someone three days ago sounds sarcastic. Also: never use the adverb form 오랜만에 as a standalone greeting — it needs a following verb.

mistakes: Using 오랜만이에요 for someone you saw very recently
It implies a genuinely long gap (weeks/months). For a short absence say 안녕하세요; using 오랜만이에요 sounds sarcastic otherwise.
Saying 오랜만에 as a standalone greeting
오랜만에 is an adverb ('after a long time') needing a verb — 오랜만에 만나요. The greeting sentence is 오랜만이에요.
Forgetting the interval-만, e.g. 오래만이에요
The correct word is 오랜만 (오래 + ㄴ + 만). Spelling it 오래만 drops the structure that signals 'after a long elapsed interval.'

usage: friendly, hopeful parting; implies you genuinely want to meet again
또 + 보다, the shorter casual version, slightly lighter
다음에 = next time; implies a real plan or intention
반말 to a close friend as you part
examples: 오늘 진짜 재밌었어. 또 봐!
Today was really fun. See ya!
반말 parting from a friend after a great time; 오늘 진짜 재밌었어 is the natural lead-in
A: 벌써 가요? 아쉽다. / B: 네, 다음에 또 만나요. 조심히 들어가세요.
A: Are you leaving already? What a shame. / B: Yes, let's meet again next time. Get home safely.
A/B farewell exchange — the most natural daily context for 또 만나요, paired with a safety send-off
좋은 인연이었어요. 기회 되면 또 만나요.
It was a good connection. Let's meet again if we get the chance.
warm but open-ended farewell; 기회 되면 ('if the opportunity arises') softens it for situations where you genuinely hope to reconnect but have no fixed plan
nuance: 또 만나요 joins 또 (again) with 만나다 (to meet, in the 요-form), meaning 'let's meet again' — a hopeful goodbye that implies you value this person and want to continue the relationship. 만나다 specifically means 'to meet up with a person' (a sought-out, intentional encounter), unlike 보다 ('to see/come across') which is lighter and more incidental; 또 봐요 uses 보다 and functions as the casual 'bye' with no specific plan behind it, while 또 만나요 feels a touch more intentional and warm. Compare 다음에 봐요 (vaguer 'see you next time'), 안녕히 가세요 (neutral farewell with no promise of reunion), and 또 만나요 (specifically projects a future meeting with genuine intent). Note 만나다 takes the person as a direct object or comitative: 친구를 만나요 / 친구와 만나요 — never 에서 for the person. The English-speaker pitfall is reflex-saying 'see you' to everyone, including strangers you will never see again; in Korean 또 만나요 genuinely implies an expectation of meeting, so for a one-off encounter where there is no plan to reconnect, the appropriate farewell is 안녕히 가세요.

structuredNuance.t: 또 (again) + 만나요 (we meet, polite). Literally 'we meet again / let's meet again.' The real connotation: a genuine forward projection of wanting to see this person again — not a throwaway farewell. It sets an expectation of reunion.

Use when parting from a friend, acquaintance, or someone you've just had a positive meeting with — and genuinely expect or hope to meet again. 반말 또 만나 for close friends. For a one-off meeting with no realistic plan, use the neutral 안녕히 가세요 instead. To a senior you're parting from: 또 뵙겠습니다 (humble 뵙다).

또 봐요 = casual 'see you,' using the lighter 보다; the parting phrase with no specific expectation. 다음에 봐요 = 'see you next time,' slightly vaguer and time-delayed. 안녕히 가세요 = neutral goodbye, no promise of reunion. 또 만나요 is the most intentional among these — it specifically projects wanting to meet the person again.
또 만나 (반말) → 또 만나요 (polite) → 또 뵙겠습니다 (humble, for seniors) → 다음에 또 만나요 (adds next-time specificity). Casual synonym: 또 봐 / 또 봐요.

English 'see you' and 'see you again' are reflexive parting fillers that can be said to strangers you will genuinely never see again. 또 만나요 in Korean projects real intent to meet — using it with someone you just met briefly and will likely never see again can feel hollow or odd. For a one-time farewell, 안녕히 가세요 is the clean choice.

mistakes: Saying 또 만나요 when you won't realistically meet again
It projects a genuine future meeting. For a one-time encounter with no plans, use 안녕히 가세요 / 안녕히 계세요 instead.
Using 보다 for arranging to meet a person, e.g. '친구를 봐요' for 'I'm meeting a friend'
보다 is 'see/look'; to actively arrange to meet a person use 만나다 — 친구를 만나요. (또 봐요 as a casual goodbye is fine, but for making plans, 만나다 is correct.)
Marking the person with 에서: 친구에서 만나요
에서 marks a location, not the person met. Use 친구를 만나요 or 친구와 만나요; 에서 is for the place (카페에서 만나요).
